articles.title: Ismael Galancho, nutricionista y entrenador: "No hace falta llegar a 10.000 pasos; a partir de 7.000 se logra gran parte del beneficio"
articles.standfirst: La cifra de pasos diarios que recomiendan los expertos está por debajo de la popular meta de los 10.000
articles.summary: La cifra de pasos diarios que recomiendan los expertos está por debajo de la popular meta de los 10.000
articles.body: Caminar es una de las formas más sencillas de aumentar la actividad física diaria y no es necesario alcanzar los 10.000 pasos para obtener buena parte de sus beneficios. El nutricionista y entrenador Ismael Galancho ha puesto el foco en una cifra inferior y ha explicado que, a partir de los 7.000 pasos diarios, se consigue "gran parte del beneficio para la salud". La cifra de 10.000 pasos se ha convertido durante años en una referencia habitual para medir la actividad física diaria, especialmente desde la popularización de las pulseras y relojes inteligentes. Sin embargo, la evidencia científica no establece que exista un umbral concreto de 10.000 pasos a partir del cual caminar pase a ser beneficioso. Galancho ha señalado que alcanzar los 7.000 pasos diarios puede ser suficiente para obtener una parte importante de los efectos positivos asociados a caminar. "A partir de los 7.000 pasos diarios se logra gran parte del beneficio para la salud; hacer 10.000 o 12.000 puede sumar, pero mucho menos", ha explicado. La diferencia es importante porque plantea un objetivo más asequible para aquellas personas que llevan una vida sedentaria o que tienen dificultades para incorporar grandes cantidades de ejercicio a su rutina. Una revisión sistemática y metaanálisis publicada en 2025 en The Lancet Public Health analizó 57 estudios que incluían datos de más de 160.000 adultos y examinó la relación entre el número de pasos diarios y diferentes resultados relacionados con la salud. Los investigadores observaron que aumentar el número de pasos estaba asociado con un menor riesgo de mortalidad y de diferentes enfermedades. El análisis identificó los 7.000 pasos diarios como una referencia especialmente relevante, ya que en comparación con caminar unos 2.000 pasos al día se asociaron con reducciones importantes del riesgo en varios indicadores de salud. En el caso de la mortalidad por cualquier causa, los investigadores observaron una asociación con un riesgo aproximadamente un 47% menor al alcanzar los 7.000 pasos frente a los 2.000. Esta cifra, sin embargo, debe interpretarse correctamente: el estudio analiza asociaciones entre actividad física y salud, por lo que no significa que caminar exactamente 7.000 pasos provoque por sí mismo una reducción del 47% de la mortalidad. Además, los beneficios no desaparecen al llegar a esa cifra. Caminar más puede seguir aportando ventajas, aunque el incremento adicional tiende a ser menor. Es decir, pasar de una actividad muy baja a una cantidad moderada de pasos puede tener un impacto mayor que aumentar después desde niveles ya elevados. La recomendación de caminar tampoco significa que exista una cifra mágica que sirva para todas las personas. La cantidad adecuada de actividad física depende de factores como la edad, el estado de salud, la condición física y el resto de actividad que se realice durante el día. De hecho, una de las principales ventajas de caminar es precisamente que puede incorporarse con relativa facilidad a la vida cotidiana. No es necesario realizar una única caminata larga para acumular los pasos. Caminar hasta el trabajo, subir escaleras, desplazarse andando para hacer recados o dar un paseo después de comer son algunas de las formas de incrementar el movimiento diario. La actividad física también puede repartirse en diferentes momentos del día. Para una persona que actualmente camina muy poco, aumentar progresivamente el número de pasos puede ser una estrategia más realista que intentar alcanzar de golpe una cifra elevada. Esto resulta especialmente relevante porque pasar de prácticamente ninguna actividad a caminar con regularidad ya supone un cambio importante. La Organización Mundial de la Salud recomienda que los adultos realicen entre 150 y 300 minutos semanales de actividad física aeróbica moderada, o entre 75 y 150 minutos de actividad intensa, además de actividades de fortalecimiento muscular al menos dos días a la semana.

articles.title: Josh Allen will wear 8 Bills hats designed by Golisano kids. Fans can buy them, too
articles.summary: Josh Allen will wear eight caps designed by Golisano Children's Hospital kids at Bills home games. Proceeds from sales benefit the Patricia Allen Fund.
articles.body:
Josh Allen provided the morose blue potato.

Nine children receiving care at Golisano Children's Hospital of Buffalo turned Allen's famously questionable attempt at drawing the Buffalo Bills logo into eight colorful caps he'll wear before home games this season.

And this time, Bills fans can wear them, too.

New Era released the eight Buffalo Bills hats as part of its 2026 Billustration Collection . Each design is available for $49.99, with proceeds benefiting the Patricia Allen Fund at Golisano Children's Hospital.

Allen will wear a different cap during his tunnel walk before each of the Bills' eight regular-season home games.

Each one features Allen's now-famous hand-drawn Bills logo on the front, with colors and original artwork created by the children stitched throughout the rest of the cap.

Allen and New Era started the Billustration project last season after the Bills quarterback expanded his partnership with the Buffalo-based company.

Allen became the first New Era ambassador to receive an investment stake in the company and was given the title "Director of Billustration." The title was inspired by Allen's attempt to draw the Bills logo from memory.

It wasn't particularly close, but it was memorable.

New Era partnered with patients at what was then Oishei Children's Hospital to create nine one-of-a-kind caps for Allen to wear before home games last season.

Those caps were later signed and auctioned, helping raise $140,230 for the Patricia Allen Fund.

The fund honors Allen's grandmother, Patricia, who died in November 2020. Bills fans responded to her death by donating more than $1 million to the children's hospital, many in $17 increments in honor of Allen's jersey number. The hospital later established the Patricia Allen Fund to support its pediatric critical care team. The fund has raised more than $17 million.

Last year's hats created another problem: Fans wanted them.

New Era and Allen solved that this season by making all eight designs available for purchase.

"I was eager to bring it back for the 2026 season in response to the demand from fans to get their hands on these special caps," Allen said in a news release.

Nobody will confuse them with the Bills' traditional red, white and blue merchandise.

"One of the most special parts of Billustration is seeing the kids' creativity come to life and learning where their inspiration comes from," Danielle Koch, executive director of the New Era Cap Foundation, said in the release. "Their imagination and perspective are incredibly powerful."

What do Josh Allen's 8 Billustration hats look like?

Josh Allen's 8 Bills hats designed by Golisano kids: See every design

Jack's cap features tan, lime green and turquoise panels, a blue brim and a turkey holding a football stitched onto the side. Allen will wear it for the home opener against the Detroit Lions on Sept. 17.

Mason went heavy on red and white and included some of his favorite things, including video games and football.

Charlotte filled her bright pink, turquoise and purple cap with things that make her happy, including rainbows, hearts and flowers. She also incorporated a pair of lungs into the design, representing a major medical challenge she overcame.

Isaac used the colors of a sunset and added a green snapback to represent kidney disease awareness.

Siblings Avery and Amar'e collaborated on a light blue and red design, combining their personalities and love of the Bills into one cap.

Killian's turquoise, tan and green cap includes an axolotl, one of his favorite animals, along with artwork representing two surgeries he underwent.

Caleb created a rainbow unicorn wearing leg braces like his own, while Grace finished the collection with a light blue design featuring a football and other Bills-inspired artwork.

Allen will wear the eight designs during home games against the Lions, Los Angeles Chargers, New England Patriots, Baltimore Ravens, Miami Dolphins, Kansas City Chiefs, Chicago Bears and New York Jets.

Where can Bills fans buy Josh Allen's Billustration hats?

The caps are available in three styles: the 9SEVENTY, 59FIFTY and a kids' 9FORTY.

The collection is available through New Era's website, the New Era Buffalo Store, New Era's SoHo flagship store, Highmark Stadium and select retailers.

articles.title: Popular diet slashes liver fat by 67% while reversing prediabetes in some people
articles.summary: A keto diet reduced liver fat by roughly 67% and reversed prediabetes in half of participants, but the study's small sample size is a caveat.
articles.body: The keto diet may have surprising benefits for liver health, a new study suggests. The research, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, studied 42 adults who had obesity, prediabetes and excess liver fat. In a randomized clinical trial, the participants were assigned to three weight-loss diets – a low-carb ketogenic diet, a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat, mostly plant-based diet. SECRET TO WEIGHT LOSS MAY BE HIDING IN YOUR GUT, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS The keto diet’s calories consisted of about 4% carbohydrates and 73% fat, according to the study. The Mediterranean diet provided about 50% of calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat, while the low-fat diet provided about 70% of calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat. In all three groups, muscle insulin sensitivity improved by about 50%, helping the muscles take up blood sugar more efficiently. Liver insulin sensitivity improved two to three times as much in the keto group as in the other diet groups. Liver fat decreased by roughly 67% among people following the keto diet, compared with about 45% among those on the other diets. The reduction was linked to a decrease in the liver’s production of new fat. Glucose and insulin measures also generally improved more in the keto group. About 50% of participants in that group no longer met the criteria for prediabetes by the end of the trial, compared with 29% of those following the Mediterranean diet and 7% of those on the low-fat diet. ONE COMMON TYPE OF FAT MAY INCREASE DIABETES RISK, WHILE ANOTHER HELPS FIGHT IT The study’s short duration and small sample size — about 14 people in each diet group — limit how broadly the findings can be applied to the general population, the researchers said. The researchers concluded that, among people with obesity, prediabetes and excess liver fat, the composition of a weight-loss diet may influence certain metabolic outcomes beyond the effects of weight loss alone. The keto diet produced the greatest improvements in liver fat and liver insulin sensitivity in this small trial. Registered dietitian nutritionist Ilana Muhlstein reflected on the study findings. "I love more and more validation and recognition that calories are not equal," the California-based expert told Fox News Digital. Muhlstein said people often reduce weight loss to "just a calorie deficit," but this study showed that differences in macronutrients were associated with different changes in health markers despite similar weight loss. POPULAR DIET TREND COULD BOOST MENTAL HEALTH AMONG OLDER ADULTS, STUDY FINDS Although weight loss occurred across all three groups, Muhlstein said the participants experienced different internal metabolic changes. The keto group showed a greater reduction in the liver’s production of new fat, along with metabolic changes consistent with greater fat burning. Muhlstein explained that excess calories and metabolic dysfunction can cause fat to accumulate in the liver, even in people who do not drink alcohol. She recommends that anyone with a fatty liver should consider transitioning to a lower carbohydrate diet. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Muhlstein said reducing carbohydrate intake may encourage the body to use more stored fat for energy. The findings were notable because the keto group did not experience higher cholesterol or blood-fat measurements during the short study, the expert noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "This is a really interesting study for someone who has prediabetes, someone who had blood sugar irregularity, but maybe still something to be cautious of if someone has heart disease in the family or is at high risk of heart disease," she added. Overall, Muhlstein said the findings suggest keto may be worth discussing as a short-term option for some people with obesity or prediabetes, particularly because the study found greater reductions in liver fat and higher rates of prediabetes remission — even though weight loss was similar across the three groups. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Keto is not something I recommend for anyone long-term because of the high saturated fat, and usually it translates into a lower-fiber diet, which is not good for heart health," Muhlstein said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So potentially, it should be something used short-term early on for someone with prediabetes, and then they can transition into Mediterranean, which would be overall helpful for your heart, your brain and so much more."

articles.title: No end to torture of Gaza doctor Abu Safia in Israeli prison: What to know
articles.summary: Abu Safia, who has been under custody for nearly two years, continues to face abuse inside prison, his lawyer says.
articles.body:
Jailed Palestinian doctor Hussam Abu Safia continues to face abuse under Israeli detention, according to his lawyer, raising renewed concerns about his safety inside the prison.

Israel abducted Abu Safia on December 27, 2024 from the Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza for defying Israeli orders to evacuate the hospital – one of the last remaining functioning medical facilities at the time. Israel has killed hundreds of medics and destroyed or damaged almost all of Gaza’s hospitals as part of its push to cripple the enclave’s healthcare system.

Campaigners and the family of the Palestinian doctor have routinely highlighted his physical state inside the prison, calling for his release. In July, a United Nations inquiry commission said Abu Sufia faced “continued and severe abuse”, and last month, the director general of Gaza’s Ministry of Health called for urgent action to “save” the jailed doctor’s life.

So what is the latest testimony by the jailed doctor, and why does Israel continue to keep him in detention without any charge?

The jailed doctor’s latest testimony was conveyed by his lawyer, Nasser Odeh, according to a statement on Wednesday by Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI). Odeh visited Abu Safia in the Rakefet detention facility inside Nitzan Prison on August 30.

Abu Safia said Israeli prison guards continue to beat him, deprive him of sleep, and threaten him against sharing the conditions of his detention with his lawyer.

Guards assault the doctor by “punching and kicking him and beating him with batons across his body, including sensitive areas”, according to the statement from PHRI.

Abu Safia is also “deliberately” deprived of sleep through the use of loudspeakers and other noise throughout the night, PHRI said.

What else has Abu Safia experienced during his detention?

Rights groups and his family have long said he shows signs of having been regularly tortured.

The doctor has been held in solitary confinement at the underground Rakefet facility, where he has been subjected to daily violence and beatings, his lawyer has said in the past.

At one point, his injuries were so severe – with “fresh and serious bruises on his head, around his eyes, on his ears, and on his neck”, that his lawyer had trouble recognising him, PHRI, the Israeli rights group, said in July.

In June, footage of Abu Safia appearing via videolink before an Israeli court showed him looking noticeably thinner in his face and around his abdomen.

On August 10, he was transferred from Rafeket to the prison service’s medical centre at Ramla prison, which PHRI has stated “in itself indicates serious medical needs that cannot be adequately addressed in ordinary prison wards”.

The jailed Gaza doctor’s testimony comes as PHRI pursues legal proceedings demanding that an independent physician examine him – a request submitted to the Israel Prison Service on July 7 but which has not yet been approved, said the organisation.

Abu Safia has also petitioned an Israeli administrative court through the group, while the Israel Prison Service recently requested additional time to submit its response.

The Israeli rights group has said “there is no justification for further delay.”

There are no charges against the doctor and he has not undergone any trial, as he is held under Israel’s unlawful combatant law – a policy it has used to hold Palestinians for prolonged periods without trial.

The Israeli forces abducted the doctor after raiding the Kamal Adwan Hospital, which was rendered destroyed. He had refused to evacuate the hospital.

Amnesty International has called the unlawful combatant law “at odds with international law”.

“This law authorises the military to issue indefinitely renewable detention orders against anyone from the Gaza Strip suspected of posing a threat to state security or engagement in hostile activities, based on classified evidence and without having to produce an indictment,” Sara Hashash, deputy regional director for the Middle East and North Africa at the organisation, told Al Jazeera.

Before his detention, he had been a prominent voice highlighting Gaza’s decimated healthcare sector during Israel’s genocide and continued to work despite the death of one of his sons in an Israeli drone attack.

At least 13 other Palestinian doctors from Gaza have been imprisoned for more than a year and a half without charges or due process, according to PHRI.

“Our central demand remains unchanged: The release of the 14 physicians from Gaza, including Dr Abu Safia, so that they can reunite with their families and resume their medical duties,” the organisation said in its statement on Wednesday.

What has been the international response to Abu Safia’s arrest?

In July, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry ⁠on the Occupied Palestinian Territory called for Israel to immediately release Abu Safia. The commission also urged Israeli authorities to provide him with immediate independent medical care.

Leading human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have also petitioned for his release and an end to his torture in Israeli custody.

“Amnesty International has expressed grave concern over reports that Dr Hussam Abu Safia has been subjected to severe physical and psychological abuse, prolonged solitary confinement, beatings and other ill-treatment in detention,” said Hashash.

“Amnesty International’s position is clear: Dr Hussam Abu Safia should be immediately and unconditionally released, as should all Palestinians who are arbitrarily detained without charge or trial,” she told Al Jazeera.

How have the Palestinians been treated inside Israeli prisons?

The UN commission’s July report found that Israeli authorities’ reported conduct towards Abu Safia reflects a broader pattern of violations that it identified in previous reports. The commission has found that torture and ill-treatment of Palestinian detainees is widespread and systematic.

It has called on Israel to end its practices of arbitrary detention and torture, and has urged that independent medical experts, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and human rights monitors be given unhindered access to places of detention.

Hashash urged international community use all available diplomatic, legal and economic measures to pressure Israel to end arbitrary detention.

“In light of Israel’s persistent disregard for international law and its lack of cooperation with UN and other international human rights mechanisms, it is crucial that all states exert diplomatic and economic pressure on Israel to release Dr Hussam Abu Safia and all Palestinians it arbitrarily detains,” she said.

According to PHRI, Israel’s policy of torture in prisons against Palestinian detainees has killed at least 105 people since October 2023.

Israel is currently holding more than 9,400 prisoners, including 92 women and more than 370 children, according to Palestinian and Israeli rights groups.

Palestinians jailed by Israel have faced widespread abuse in custody , including routine beatings, starvation and sexual assault. Former Palestinian detainees have told Al Jazeera how they suffered dehumanising treatment by guards and soldiers, including torture and sexual violence.

articles.title: Qualcomm backs Ultrahuman in $70M round on bet to turn smart rings into computers
articles.summary: Ultrahuman is targeting a $200 million annual revenue run rate by January 2027 as it builds a new Qualcomm-powered smart ring.
articles.body:
Ultrahuman , an Indian startup best known for making smart rings, has raised $70 million in a new funding round that includes backing from Qualcomm’s venture arm, as it looks beyond sleep and health tracking to build a ring that can run software on the device and eventually power everything from AI interactions to games.

The round values Bengaluru-based Ultrahuman at $365 million, about 3x its $120 million valuation in 2023, a person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch.

Qualcomm Ventures participated in the financing alongside U.S. diagnostics giant Labcorp, Alpha Wave, Blume Ventures, Nexus Venture Partners, and Alteria Capital. The round includes $65 million in primary equity and $5 million in debt, Ultrahuman founder and CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview.

Ultrahuman is also working with Qualcomm on a new ring that will use the U.S. chipmaker’s silicon, Kumar told TechCrunch. The startup currently uses chips from Nordic Semiconductor in its rings and plans to continue using them alongside Qualcomm’s technology. The added computing power will allow more software and algorithms to run directly on the ring, reducing its reliance on a phone or the cloud, he said.

“All ring devices today are like trackers,” Kumar said. “You put on the ring, it measures your heart rate, your movement, your sleep.” Ultrahuman’s goal, he stated, is to make the ring more like a computer, where programs and algorithms can run on the device itself.

This could open the ring to use cases well beyond health and sleep tracking, something Ultrahuman rings are known for.

Developers, Kumar said, could eventually write their own programs for the device, while Ultrahuman is exploring ways for the ring to work as a pointer or mouse, a game controller, a car key, and an interface for interacting with AI.

“The future of AI is personal, ambient, and always on,” said Quinn Li, global head of Qualcomm Ventures, adding that Ultrahuman is building a new generation of “personal AI devices.”

While the Qualcomm-powered ring is planned to come later, Ultrahuman is not waiting for the new hardware to start testing that idea. Kumar told TechCrunch that some of the new capabilities will arrive on the startup’s existing Ring Air and Ring Pro (pictured above) through a software update by the end of September, including features that would let the ring work as a game controller and interact with AI applications. It will also have the ability to allow third-party developers to build new features.

Ultrahuman’s idea is to take advantage of the ring’s position on a user’s finger, Kumar said. Unlike a smartwatch, which he described as more akin to “a phone on the wrist,” a ring could act as a precise pointing and interaction device while also carrying physiological context such as a user’s heart rate, temperature, and movement.

“A game controller never reads your heart rate and your temperature, but this one does,” Kumar said. He continued by imagining games that could respond not only to a player’s movements but also to signals such as their heart rate and body temperature, making the ring both a controller and a source of physiological context.

Meanwhile, Ultrahuman’s existing business is growing even as the startup looks to expand what its rings can do. The startup, Kumar said, is currently at an annual revenue run rate of $140 million, up roughly 45% from a year earlier, and expects that run rate to reach $200 million by January 2027. It has sold around 800,000 rings to date, up from about 700,000 in February, Kumar mentioned. About 12% of its users also pay for PowerPlugs, Ultrahuman’s subscription-based software features.

Co-founded by Kumar and Vatsal Singhal in 2019, Ultrahuman initially debuted with its continuous glucose monitors to help people track their metabolic health. The startup, however, later moved into smart rings, which have since become the mainstay of its business. It also introduced blood testing and environmental sensing to build a broader health platform.

The U.S. remains Ultrahuman’s largest market, though the startup had to stop selling its Ring Air here for much of the past year following a patent dispute with rival Oura. Ultrahuman returned to the market with its redesigned Ring Pro this year. Demand for the new device, Kumar said, is currently running at 18x to 20x the startup’s available supply in the U.S.

Kumar told TechCrunch that the startup expects to return to its previous U.S. sales volumes as soon as next quarter and aims to triple those volumes over the following four quarters as it ramps up supply. The U.S. has accounted for about 45% of Ultrahuman’s revenue this quarter, while India contributes about 11%, Kumar said.

Ultrahuman plans to use some of the new capital to deepen its presence in markets, including India and the UAE, where it has found that physical stores and other offline touchpoints can help drive sales. However, that expansion, along with spending on clinical research and product development, has come at a cost. Ultrahuman, Kumar said, may not be profitable this year after investing more heavily in physical locations, its brand, and clinical studies.

Unlike rival Oura, which is reportedly eyeing a September IPO , a public listing is still some way off for Ultrahuman. Kumar told TechCrunch that the startup wants to demonstrate about eight quarters of profitability before going public, a track record he expects could take eight to 10 quarters to establish. However, he sees 2028 as the earliest window for an IPO.

In the meantime, Ultrahuman is also looking to work more closely with Labcorp, as it tries to push its rings deeper into health and diagnostics. The companies, Kumar said, are exploring whether the blood-flow signals captured by the ring, when paired with blood-test data, could help identify health risks in areas including cardiovascular health, fertility, and aging.

“By combining longitudinal wearable data with deeper biological signals, Ultrahuman is creating new opportunities in personalized health,” said Megann Vaughn Watters, vice president and head of Labcorp Venture Fund and Strategic Alliances.

The partnership could eventually lead to integrations with Ultrahuman’s products, Kumar said, though he declined to share details, adding that the startup expects to have more to announce soon.

articles.title: Deadly mosquito-borne virus claims first life in major US city as cases spread
articles.summary: Chicago's first West Nile virus death of 2026 follows the city's rainiest summer in years, as CDPH sprays insecticide across 15 community areas.
articles.body: A Chicago resident has died from West Nile virus, marking the city’s first death linked to the mosquito-borne illness this year, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. Several other cases have been reported throughout Illinois. The virus is most commonly spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito, although the disease cycle also includes infected birds. When mosquitoes feed on infected birds, they can pick up the virus and transmit it to humans. 2 AIRPORT WORKERS ARE DEAD AFTER MALARIA CASES SHOCK OFFICIALS AT MAJOR TRAVEL HUB "2026 has seen the rainiest summer in Chicago in years, giving mosquitoes ample opportunities to breed," CDPH Commissioner Garth Walker said in a statement. "The best way to protect yourself from West Nile virus is to avoid mosquito bites and take measures to stop them from breeding around your home." In an attempt to prevent infections, the CDPH has sprayed insecticide in the following community areas: Beverly, Burnside, Chatham, East Garfield Park, the Lower West Side, Morgan Park, the Near West Side, North Lawndale, O'Hare, Pullman, Roseland, South Deering, Washington Heights, West Lawn and West Pullman. Symptoms and treatment For most people, West Nile produces mild symptoms — such as fever, aches and rashes — or none at all, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. VACATION HOT SPOT FACES NEW CDC TRAVEL WARNING AS OUTBREAK CASES CONTINUE CLIMBING In rare serious cases, the virus invades the nervous system, causing meningitis, encephalitis (swelling of the brain), paralysis or death. People over 50 or those with compromised immune systems are at highest risk, experts caution. "Of those who do have symptoms, about 20%, maybe 25%, will have the flu-like symptoms — fever, headache, body aches — and it’s very hard to distinguish between that and flu," Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES There are also rare, severe neuroinvasive cases, when the virus infects the brain. "When there's inflammation that leads to meningitis or encephalitis, that's very bad," warned Evans, who is also the CEO and chief medical officer for Wellness Equity Alliance. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "So if there's ever any severe headaches, stiff neck, disorientation, vision loss, feeling like you're just really confused, and if you're over the age of 65, or have immunocompromising conditions like severe diabetes or cancers, that's when you're going to want to seek emergency management as quickly as possible." While there are no vaccines or specific treatments for West Nile virus, there are supportive treatments. "For the flu-like symptoms, generally speaking, if you're not over the age of 65 and you're not immunocompromised, you don't have to go to the emergency room," Evans advised. "But if you are over the age of 65 and/or have those immunocompromising conditions, and you're starting to experience confusion, headache, stiff neck … ER immediately, [call] 911." Prevention tips Avoiding mosquito bites is the first line of defense, according to Evans. "In areas where there are a lot of mosquitoes, DEET is going to be key," he said, recommending repellents that are at least 30% DEET for adults. In high-burden mosquito areas, he also recommends avoiding the outdoors during sundown. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Health officials also recommend wearing loose, long-sleeved clothing; applying insect repellent (especially at dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most active); and ensuring that window screens are secure. Around homes, eliminating standing water (like that found in buckets, tires and gutters) can help keep mosquitoes from breeding. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ There have been 407 reported human cases of West Nile virus in the U.S. this year, including 285 severe neuroinvasive cases and 23 deaths, according to the latest preliminary CDC data, current as of Sept. 1. Most West Nile cases are reported in August and September.

articles.title: NI health: Minister announces expert committee to review health services
articles.summary: Robbie Butler says the reconfiguration committee will provide him with advice on major or controversial proposals.
articles.body:
A new independent expert advisory committee is to review how services will be delivered across hospitals in Northern Ireland.

Health minister Robbie Butler said the Reconfiguration Committee will provide him with advice on major or controversial proposals for permanent changes to health and social care services.

It follows a major political and public row around the future of Emergency General Surgery at Causeway Hospital which triggered the resignation of Mike Nesbitt .

Announcing the move on Thursday, Butler said it will bring together independent clinical and public-interest expertise.

"Crucially, it will be able to scrutinise the evidence underpinning proposals rather than simply accepting that evidence at face value.

"It will consider patient safety, service quality, clinical effectiveness, and long-term sustainability," the minister said.

BBC News NI understands that the committee will be made up of health professionals most likely from outside of Northern Ireland who will provide independent advice on how health trusts should proceed.

It is expected that a panel will review evidence already gathered from public consultations including recommendations made in previous reports from several Royal Colleges and Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) teams.

There have been several major reviews and inquiries into the Northern Ireland Health and Social Care Service (NIHSCS) which included the number of hospitals in NI and the duplication of some services across hospital sites.

They include the Bengoa , Donaldson Reviews, Transforming Your Care and the Hayes review in 2001.

Butler said the committee's advice will be provided directly to him as minister and in the interests of transparency and accountability that advice will be published.

Dr Alan Stout, who chairs the British Medical Association's (BMA) Northern Ireland Council, said the establishment of the new committee had come as a surprise.

"We actually haven't been consulted on it or it hasn't been discussed with us before," he told BBC News NI.

"There is a real scepticism that the last thing that we need is yet another committee, more reports and more evidence, whenever we have a wealth of evidence, a wealth of reports that are telling us and have been telling us for 10 years what we need to do."

He said the committee can not be "another layer of review" at a time when "definitive decisions" needed to be taken quickly.

"We are seeing massive problems right across our service, right across every trust, every hospital, general practice," he said.

"We're seeing transformation by collapse at the moment."

Sinn Féin MLA Philip McGuigan, who chairs Stormont's health committee, said the proposed reconfiguration committee "could ensure public confidence in future decisions".

That, he said, was dependent on it being "genuinely independent, has access to all relevant evidence and ensures the voices of clinicians, patients, healthcare workers and local communities are heard."

He said he will now ask for further detail on its remit, membership and the timeframe for establishing the new committee.

McGuigan added; "We need reform, but it must be properly funded, planned on a whole-system basis and undertaken with the best for patient outcomes, regardless of where they live, as the desired outcome."

Alliance MLA Nuala McAllister said Butler's decision to establish a new committee proves he is a "caretaker health minister who will dodge difficult decisions".

"We urgently need to drive forward reconfiguration with evidence-based decision-making, and bring people with us on that journey through strong political leadership.

"Instead, we have more dither, delay and risk of unplanned service collapse," she said.

BBC News NI understands that the Department of Health had been planning to announce this panel several weeks ago but was finalising who might lead it.

Its understood the search was on for someone outside of Northern Ireland and who is not a politician.

While such a plan would have taken the politics out of health in the short term – Robbie Butler will still have the final say on what happens in the future.

Whether this committee or panel will have delivered their final report before next May's election is questionable.

There have been huge attempts to transform health and particularly hospital services for the past number of years.

This announcement of another independent committee will no doubt leave some people scratching their heads.

Does it feel like Northern Ireland is delaying the inevitable yet again or deferring the difficult decisions yet again – it is hard to argue any differently.

articles.title: Marijuana users may face hidden driving danger that standard tests can miss
articles.summary: Cannabis edible users registered THC levels nearly 10 times lower than smokers despite similar driving impairment, exposing a potential road safety gap.
articles.body: A new study warns that driving after eating cannabis edibles can significantly impair road performance and reaction times, even if blood tests show THC levels far below the legal limit. The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, highlight a potential challenge for impaired-driving enforcement in Canada and some U.S. jurisdictions. Most previous cannabis-driving studies have involved smoked or inhaled marijuana, which more rapidly spikes levels of THC (tetrahydrocannabinol, the main psychoactive compound in cannabis) in the bloodstream. AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING Edibles are absorbed more slowly and can produce driving impairment even when blood THC concentrations remain relatively low. Researchers found that drivers who consumed higher doses of edible THC struggled with lane control, had slower reaction times and experienced greater speed fluctuations. Yet, their blood tests stayed below the standard legal cutoff used to prove impairment at roadside traffic stops. To assess how oral cannabis impacts driving, researchers at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto conducted a trial with 40 healthy adult volunteers who regularly use cannabis. Each participant attended four separate sessions in which they consumed soft-chew gummies containing either 0, 2, 10 or 20 milligrams of THC. CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS The researchers then tested the drivers using a driving simulator at two, five and 24 hours after consumption, tracking how well drivers stayed in their lane, how quickly they reacted to road events and how consistently they maintained their speed. Blood samples and self-reported ratings of intoxication were also collected. The results showed driving impairment at two and five hours after consuming 10- and 20-milligram gummies. Compared with placebo, participants who consumed those doses had greater variability in lane position, while the 20-milligram dose was also linked to slower reaction times and less consistent speed control. Participants also recognized their own limitations, reporting a lower willingness to drive and reduced confidence in their driving skills after taking the gummies. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The highest blood THC concentrations averaged 1.6 nanograms per milliliter after the 10-milligram dose and 3.4 nanograms per milliliter after the 20-milligram dose. Those levels were below the commonly used 5-ng/mL threshold, although THC limits vary by jurisdiction and some individual samples exceeded 5 ng/mL. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER By comparison, participants in the team’s previous smoked-cannabis study showed similar levels of impairment while reaching an average peak blood THC concentration of 30.3 nanograms per milliliter, nearly 10 times higher than the 20-milligram edible group. The study did have some limitations. Tests were conducted on virtual simulators rather than actual roads, meaning drivers faced no real physical risk during the experiments. It also focused on regular cannabis users, so it is unclear how occasional users might react to similar doses. Additionally, minimal residual effects were detected after 24 hours. While maximum speed remained slightly higher among participants on the 10-milligram and 20-milligram doses, subjective feelings of intoxication had completely faded. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In an accompanying commentary, Dr. José Ignacio Nazif-Munoz of the Université de Sherbrooke noted that these biological differences pose a challenge for law enforcement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Because edibles are absorbed slowly through the digestive system, standard blood tests may fail to identify unsafe drivers, leaving policymakers searching for more reliable roadside tools. "The delayed absorption and prolonged duration of effects of edible cannabis distinguish it from smoked or inhaled cannabis, complicating the interpretation of biological measures," he wrote.

articles.title: Oura files to go public
articles.summary: The ring maker says that its business has shown significant revenue growth over the past year.
articles.body:
Oura, the smart ring maker, has filed to go public.

The filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday shows that Oura’s revenue has jumped substantially in the past year. The company went from $697 million in revenue during the nine-month period that ended June 30 last year to $1.2 billion during the corresponding period this year.

The company has said previously that it generated $500 million in revenue in 2024, roughly $1 billion in 2025, and that it expected to generate close to $2 billion in revenue this year.

The company says it has sold 3.6 million rings over the past year, and that it currently has approximately 5 million paid members — that is, users who subscribe to its service for broader health metrics. The filing also says that Oura has an approximately 85% weighted-average 12-month membership retention rate, meaning that roughly 85% of members who sign up in a given month are still subscribed a year later.

The company’s rings, which sell in the range of $350 to $400, are, at their most fundamental level, fitness trackers designed to measure a user’s biometrics — everything from metabolism and heart rate to stress levels and sleep patterns. Paired with an app, the ring and that software are marketed by Oura as an “always-on health intelligence platform.”

Late last month, it was reported that Oura was looking to raise $3 billion during its expected public offering. The company, which was founded in Finland in 2013, confidentially filed for an IPO in May. Bloomberg previously reported that the company is expected to seek a $16 billion valuation. In October of last year, it had been valued at around $11 billion .

In its SEC filing, Oura outlines where it believes its audience can widen in the coming years. “We believe our opportunity extends beyond traditional wearable use cases centered on activity and fitness tracking,” it says. “We believe our platform can support significantly larger populations as we continue to expand access, build clinical evidence, and deepen integrations with health plans, employers, and care providers.”

Oura also notes how its trove of data is fueling new AI integrations. “We believe we have amassed one of the largest and highest-quality longitudinal biometric datasets in consumer health, tracking over 50 health and wellness metrics and representing nearly 42 billion hours of physiological data,” it states. “This dataset powers our AI and machine-learning models, which decode complex physiological patterns and improve in accuracy, personalization, and predictive capability as member histories deepen.”

TechCrunch has reached out to Oura for more information.

The company, which now has offices throughout the world, including San Francisco, was recently hit with a proposed class action lawsuit accusing it of misleading users about the accuracy of its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit alleges Oura’s rings can’t actually detect the physiological signals needed to determine sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that the complaint describes as little more reliable than a coin flip. The litigation follows years of online complaints from users who said that Oura consistently rated their sleep as optimal when, in fact, it was not.

The company has disputed the allegations and previously told TechCrunch it will “defend against” the claims in the “appropriate legal forum.”
